consensus_summary: Sheol is the OT term for the common realm/abode/state of the dead (grave or underworld) to which all—righteous and wicked—descend; a shadowy, silent condition of death itself (intermediate prior to resurrection, = Hades), not a place of active/final punishment and distinct from Gehenna. Consciousness, divisions, and exact duration remain disputed across traditions; personification and eventual emptying/destruction appear in supporting texts and alternatives.
book_summary: Sheol is the demanding place (from sha'al ‘to demand’): mortality’s claim on all flesh that swallows righteous and wicked alike, personified with mouth, gates and bars. Its dead sleep in silence until released; then Sheol itself is destroyed. Distinct from Gehenna the judgment.
consensus_core_identification: common abode/state of the dead (grave/underworld) for all people, shadowy/silent, intermediate, not final hell/Gehenna
book_core_identification: mortality’s demanding/personified claim that swallows all flesh; dead sleep silently until released, after which Sheol is destroyed; not Gehenna
boundary_disagreement: Book elevates silent sleep of the dead and Sheol’s own destruction after release to definitional status (and centers etymological ‘demand’ plus gates/bars), whereas consensus primary leaves consciousness/divisions open among traditions and treats destruction/emptying as eventual but secondary; thus book reclassifies the intermediate state more narrowly as sleep and temporary.
rationale: Minimum cores identify the same central referent—the place/state claiming all the dead, personified in places, intermediate and distinct from Gehenna—so the category is preserved. Extra detail does not replace it. Book nevertheless refines precision and boundary conditions by making ‘demand,’ universal swallow, silent sleep, release, and destruction of Sheol itself essential rather than optional or alternative, thereby reclassifying the nature and terminus of the intermediate state relative to the broader consensus range.
strongest_objection: Etymology from sha'al ‘demand’ is speculative (not the dominant scholarly derivation); ‘sleep in silence’ privileges the conditionalist/soul-sleep reading over common bipartite-conscious alternatives that consensus still lists.
